primary_source.title: National Curriculum in England: Mathematics Programmes of Study

expectations: Represent and use number bonds and related subtraction facts within 20.
Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero.
Solve one-step addition and subtraction problems with concrete objects, pictorial representations and missing-number forms.
Solve one-step multiplication and division problems using concrete objects, pictorial representations and arrays with teacher support.
Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently and derive related facts to 100.
Add and subtract two-digit numbers using concrete, pictorial and mental methods.
Use the inverse relationship to check calculations and solve missing-number problems.
addition_subtraction.written_method_status: Recording in columns supports place value and prepares pupils for later formal written methods.

expectations: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 multiplication tables.
Represent multiplication and division using signs and equations.
Solve problems using materials, arrays, repeated addition, mental methods and known facts.
Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and ones, tens or hundreds.
Add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal columnar addition and subtraction.
Estimate and use inverse operations to check answers.
Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 tables.
Calculate two-digit by one-digit multiplication, moving from mental approaches toward formal written methods.
Develop reliable written multiplication and division methods beginning with two-digit by one-digit calculations.
multiplication_division.written_method_status: Transition year: mental and derived facts are explicitly connected to emerging written methods.

expectations: Add and subtract numbers with up to four digits using formal columnar methods where appropriate.
Estimate and use inverse operations to check calculations.
Choose operations and methods in two-step contextual problems.
Recall multiplication and division facts up to 12 × 12.
Use place value and known/derived facts for mental multiplication and division.
Multiply two- and three-digit numbers by one digit using formal written layout.
Practise short multiplication and short division with exact answers.
Add and subtract whole numbers with more than four digits using formal columnar methods.
Calculate mentally with increasingly large numbers.
Use rounding to check answers and judge appropriate accuracy.
Multiply up to four-digit numbers by one- or two-digit numbers using formal written methods, including long multiplication for two-digit multipliers.
Divide up to four-digit numbers by one digit using short division and interpret remainders in context.
Use factors, multiples, primes, square and cube numbers in calculation and problem solving.
Use formal columnar addition and subtraction with larger numbers as part of fluent four-operation calculation.
Solve multi-step contextual problems and use estimation to check reasonableness.
Multiply up to four-digit numbers by a two-digit whole number using long multiplication.
Divide up to four-digit numbers by a two-digit whole number using long division and short division where appropriate.
Interpret remainders as whole-number remainders, fractions or rounded values according to context.
Perform mental calculations involving mixed operations and large numbers.
multiplication_division.end_of_stage_signal: By the end of Year 6 pupils should be fluent in written methods for all four operations.

mathbridge_interpretation.core_pattern: England delays formal algorithms until conceptual, mental and representational foundations have been established, then makes formal written methods increasingly explicit from Year 3 onward.
mathbridge_interpretation.comparison_warning: The statutory programmes are written year-by-year, but schools have flexibility within each key stage; MathBridge should therefore label these as statutory year expectations, not mandatory week-by-week sequencing.
